title: Ch. 7 Textbook Problems

ch7-1.5.title: Andover Bank vs Lowell Bank CDs
ch7-1.5.body: You deposit $1,000 in a 1-year CD at each bank at the beginning of 2024, and reinvest the principal plus interest in a new 1-year CD at the end of 2024 and again at the end of 2025.

ch7-1.6.title: US real GDP per capita, 2018–2022
ch7-1.6.body: Real GDP per capita for the United States (2017 dollars).

ch7-1.7.title: Health gains in southern Africa and Egypt
ch7-1.7.body: Easterly reports that a measles vaccination campaign in seven southern African nations (from 1996) virtually eliminated measles by 2000, and that an Egyptian campaign promoting oral rehydration therapy (1982–1989) cut childhood deaths from diarrhea by 82%.

ch7-1.8.title: Do institutions flow like water or bricks?
ch7-1.8.body: Charles Kenny argues that process technologies, such as institutions like laws and inventory management systems, “flow less like water and more like bricks,” while ideas and inventions (the importance of education, vaccines) “really might flow more easily across borders and over distances.”

ch7-2.1.title: Per-worker production function
ch7-2.1.body: The per-worker production function relates real GDP per hour worked (Y/L) to capital per hour worked (K/L), holding technology constant (Figures 7.3 and 7.4).

ch7-2.2.title: Diminishing returns to capital
ch7-2.2.body: Answer both parts about diminishing returns to capital in the growth model.

ch7-2.4.title: Knowledge capital and R&D
ch7-2.4.body: Questions on knowledge capital and the role of government in promoting it.

ch7-2.6.title: China's per-worker production function
ch7-2.6.body: Decide whether each scenario results in a movement along, or a shift of, China's per-worker production function.

ch7-2.8.title: Samuelson and the Soviet economy
ch7-2.8.body: In the 1961 edition of his textbook, Paul Samuelson noted that Soviet GDP might become larger than US GDP by 1985.

ch7-2.9.title: Shifts in the production function
ch7-2.9.body: Refer to the textbook graph with three per-worker production functions: production function₁ (lowest), ₂ (middle) and ₃ (highest). Points A, B and C lie on production functions 1, 2 and 3 respectively, **directly above one another at the same level of capital per hour worked (K/L)**. The vertical axis is real GDP per hour worked (Y/L).

ch7-2.12.title: Creative destruction in America
ch7-2.12.body: Alan Greenspan and Adrian Wooldridge argue that “the key to America's success lies in its unique toleration for ‘creative destruction,’ the destabilizing force described by the economist Joseph Schumpeter in 1942.”

ch7-2.13.title: Romer: it's good that the Portuguese exist
ch7-2.13.body: In the traditional theory of trade, England and Portugal both benefit because each has a comparative advantage in a different good. Paul Romer says that in the new growth theory, more people, even remote ones, are good to have around because “they might discover something valuable.” He concludes: “The new insight is that ‘It's good that the Portuguese exist.’”

ch7-3.6.title: Is the productivity slowdown a measurement problem?
ch7-3.6.body: Some economists argue that the slowdown in productivity growth is due to measurement difficulties: standard techniques are “insufficient to capture the massive benefits” of things like algorithmic recommendations for streaming videos. Before the internet, finding facts required a trip to the library; now a Google search takes seconds.

ch7-3.7.title: Secular stagnation and the loanable funds market
ch7-3.7.body: “Secular stagnation” refers to a long period of weak growth with persistently low private demand (low investment demand and high desired saving).

ch7-3.8.title: Blanchard on secular stagnation
ch7-3.8.body: Olivier Blanchard (2023): secular stagnation “refers to economies suffering from structurally low private demand,” and “global secular stagnation was and is driven by deep structural factors that neither COVID nor inflation have done anything to reverse.”

ch7-4.1.title: Catch-up
ch7-4.1.body: Questions on economic catch-up between poor and rich countries.

ch7-4.2.title: FDI vs foreign portfolio investment
ch7-4.2.body: Questions on the two forms of foreign investment.

ch7-4.3.title: Globalization
ch7-4.3.body: Questions on globalization and developing countries.

ch7-4.6.title: Matching groups of countries with graphs
ch7-4.6.body: Each of three graphs shows the average relationship between a country's initial real GDP per capita (horizontal axis) and its growth rate (vertical axis): **Graph 1** is a flat line (growth unrelated to initial income); **Graph 2** slopes downward (poorer countries grow faster); **Graph 3** slopes slightly upward (richer countries grow slightly faster).

ch7-4.7.title: McCloskey: thoroughgoing innovation
ch7-4.7.body: Deirdre McCloskey argued, “A poor country that adopts thoroughgoing innovation . . . can get within hailing distance of the West . . . in about two generations.” A generation is about 25 years. Real GDP per capita in 2021: Italy about **$31,506**, Haiti about **$1,283** (2010 US dollars). Suppose Haiti's average annual growth rate rises to **6.5%** for the next 50 years. Use: Real GDP per capita₂₀₂₁ × (1 + g)⁵⁰ = Real GDP per capita₂₀₇₁.

ch7-4.8.title: Mexico's growth forecast
ch7-4.8.body: The Bank of Mexico said that GDP is now projected to grow by 2.3% in 2023, compared with a previous forecast of 1.6%.

ch7-4.9.title: Growth prospects for Mexico
ch7-4.9.body: The Economist reported that Santiago Levy believes Mexico could enjoy annual growth of around 4% if it became more business-friendly and invested in infrastructure. A Bank of Mexico deputy governor said: “Currently, it is predominantly domestic issues holding back [foreign] investment.”

ch7-4.10.title: Tim Cook on globalization
ch7-4.10.body: Apple CEO Tim Cook said globalization is “great for the world . . . countries in the world . . . that isolate themselves, it's not good for their people.”

ch7-4.11.title: The decline in world trade
ch7-4.11.body: A 2023 Wall Street Journal article noted: “World trade as a share of overall economic activity peaked at 61% in 2008 . . . Trade has since receded to 57% of economic activity.”

ch7-5.3.title: Santiago Levy's proposals for Mexico
ch7-5.3.body: Levy thinks Mexico “needs to replace restrictions on firing with unemployment insurance and shift the tax burden away from payrolls, abolish tax perks for small firms and take contract enforcement more seriously. The prize would be faster growth . . . and better-paid jobs.”

ch7-5.4.title: China's investment in residential property
ch7-5.4.body: A Wall Street Journal article noted that China's rapidly increasing investment in residential property, particularly apartment houses, may “boost economic growth but restrain the country's long-term potential.”

ch7-5.5.title: Rule of law in China
ch7-5.5.body: Chen Guangcheng asserts that “there is no rule of law under the rule of the Chinese Communist Party.”

ch7-5.6.title: Policies to raise growth in Canada
ch7-5.6.body: Decide whether each policy is likely to raise the rate of economic growth in Canada.

ch7-5.7.title: A free press and growth
ch7-5.7.body: George Ayittey noted that of the 54 African countries only 8 had a free press, and argued strongly for establishing one to aid Africa's economic development.

ch7-5.8.title: Aid versus investment
ch7-5.8.body: Akinwumi Adesina, president of the African Development Bank: “Africa is not going to be developed by aid. It will be developed by investment.”

ch7-5.9.title: Tariffs on Chinese imports
ch7-5.9.body: Starting in 2018 the United States imposed tariffs on about $300 billion of goods imported from China. A 2023 US International Trade Commission study found that US firms and households paid higher prices for Chinese imports, rising dollar-for-dollar with the tariffs.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines “creative destruction” and its role in economic growth?

options.text: The process by which new, better products and production methods replace existing ones, putting old firms and jobs out of business; it raises living standards by moving resources to higher-productivity uses
Government destruction of obsolete factories so that new ones can be built, which raises growth by increasing the capital stock
A fall in output during a recession that clears out inefficient firms; it has no lasting effect on growth
The wearing out of capital through depreciation, which must be replaced before any growth can occur

questions.explanation: Joseph Schumpeter's term: **entrepreneurs introduce qualitatively better products and methods that replace existing ones**. Old firms, products and jobs are destroyed, but the economy's productivity and standard of living rise over time. It is a market process, not a government programme, and it is not the same thing as depreciation or a recession.

source.note: The 48% figure is illustrative; the textbook question gives no data.

questions.prompt: Real GDP rose by a total of 48% between 2007 and 2023 (16 years). How does this total increase compare with the average annual growth rate over the same period?

options.text: They are the same number, because both describe the change in real GDP between 2007 and 2023
The total is the cumulative change over all 16 years; the average annual growth rate is the much smaller yearly rate that, compounded, produces that total
The average annual growth rate is the total increase multiplied by 16
The average annual rate uses only the final year's growth, while the total uses all years

questions.explanation: The **total percentage increase** is the cumulative change from start to end, (RGDP₂₀₂₃ − RGDP₂₀₀₇)/RGDP₂₀₀₇. The **average annual growth rate** is the per-year rate that, compounded over the period, delivers that total: here about 1.48^(1/16) − 1 ≈ 2.5% a year (the shortcut 48 ÷ 16 = 3% overstates it because of compounding).

questions.prompt: Shiue and Keller found that in 1770 market efficiency in England (prices equalised across regions, allowing for transport costs) was significantly greater than in the rest of Europe and China. How does this relate to Douglass North's argument about why the Industrial Revolution began in England?

options.text: It contradicts North: efficient markets show that natural resources, not institutions, explain England's early growth
It is unrelated to North, whose argument is that England had the largest population and so the most workers

It supports North: England's institutions (secure property rights, enforceable contracts, a government that would not seize gains) encouraged entrepreneurs to trade and invest, which favoured long-run growth
It supports North because English prices were higher, which gave firms larger profits

questions.explanation: North argued that the Industrial Revolution began in England because its **institutions** (rule of law, property rights, contract enforcement) gave entrepreneurs confidence that they could keep the gains from trade and innovation. Greater market efficiency in 1770 is exactly what you would expect where trade is protected by such institutions, so the finding supports his argument.

source.note: Parts (a) and (b) are not included: the real GDP table did not come through legibly in the source file, so only part (c) is asked.

questions.prompt: Real GDP is measured in each country's own currency, and each country uses a different base year (Mexico 2013, France 2014, United States 2017). Does this matter when comparing the countries' economic growth rates?

options.text: Yes: growth rates cannot be compared unless every country uses the same currency and base year
Yes: a country with a more recent base year will always show a higher growth rate
No, but only because exchange rates are fixed between the three currencies
No: a growth rate is a percentage change, so it is unit-free; currency and base year do not matter for comparing growth rates (although they would for comparing levels of real GDP)

questions.explanation: A **growth rate is a percentage change**, so the units cancel: (RGDP₂ − RGDP₁)/RGDP₁ is the same whether real GDP is in pesos, euros or dollars. The base year changes the *level* of real GDP, not the growth rate in any meaningful way. Levels in different currencies cannot be compared directly, but growth rates can.

questions.prompt: How much interest (in dollars) have you earned on the Andover Bank CDs by the end of 2026?
How much interest (in dollars) have you earned on the Lowell Bank CDs by the end of 2026?
At the end of 2026, on which CDs will you have earned more interest?

options.text: Andover Bank: $157.63 compared with $156.88 at Lowell
Lowell Bank, because its rate is highest in the last year
They are equal, because both banks' rates average 5% over the three years
Lowell Bank, because its rates are rising

questions.explanation: Both sets of rates have a simple average of 5% ((2 + 6 + 7)/3 = 5), but compounding does not use the simple average. The ending balance is the *product* of the growth factors (1.02 × 1.06 × 1.07 = 1.1569 vs 1.05³ = 1.1576), and the order of the years does not matter. Uneven rates give a slightly smaller product than equal rates with the same average, so Lowell earns less ($156.88 vs $157.63). Equal simple averages do not give equal compounded growth.

questions.prompt: What was the percentage change in real GDP per capita between 2018 and 2022? (percent, 1 decimal)
questions.explanation: (65,415 − 61,418)/61,418 × 100 = **6.5%**. This is the total change over the four years.

questions.prompt: Using the textbook's shortcut for short periods (average the yearly growth rates), what was the average annual growth rate in real GDP per capita between 2018 and 2022? (percent, 1 decimal)
Is real GDP per capita likely to have increased significantly because of these health gains, and could the standard of living still have risen?

options.text: Yes, real GDP per capita must have risen significantly, because a healthier population always raises GDP per capita by the same proportion

Probably not by much, since these low-cost programmes mainly saved lives rather than added measured output; but living standards could still have risen substantially because GDP does not measure the value of saving children's lives
No, and living standards could not have risen either, because the standard of living is measured only by real GDP per capita
Yes, because lower child mortality directly increases the goods and services produced per person in the first year

questions.explanation: Vaccination and oral rehydration programmes cost little and mostly save lives, so **real GDP per capita need not change much**. Yet reduced child mortality plainly improves well-being: **real GDP per capita is only a proxy for the standard of living**, and health is part of the standard of living that GDP does not capture.

questions.prompt: Which seems more achievable for a developing country in the short run?

options.text: Sustained increases in real GDP per capita, because they only require more machines
They are equally hard, because both require rich-country incomes first

Eliminating measles and childhood deaths from diarrhea, because they use low-cost, well-known technologies that can spread across borders, whereas sustained growth requires hard-to-copy institutional change
Neither is achievable until the country has caught up to the high-income countries

questions.explanation: Easterly's point (and Kenny's in 1.8): **ideas and inexpensive technologies flow across borders readily**, so health improvements are quick wins, while sustained growth requires good institutions, rule of law, education and investment, which take decades to build.

questions.prompt: If Kenny is correct, what are the implications for the ability of low-income countries to rapidly increase their growth rates of real GDP per capita?

options.text: It will be easy: ideas flow freely, so every low-income country can quickly match rich-country growth rates
It will be impossible, because no knowledge can ever cross borders
Growth rates will rise quickly only if low-income countries stop using foreign ideas
It will be hard: the institutions that sustain growth spread slowly, so rapid and lasting increases in growth rates are difficult

questions.explanation: Sustained growth depends heavily on institutions (rule of law, property rights, good management). If those move like bricks, **low-income countries cannot adopt them quickly**, so fast, sustained increases in growth rates are hard.

questions.prompt: What are the implications for their ability to increase their standards of living?

options.text: Standards of living can still improve faster than growth does, because ideas such as vaccines and education move easily across borders even when institutions do not
Standards of living cannot rise unless growth rates rise first
Standards of living will fall, because ideas flow to the countries with the best institutions
Nothing changes, because standards of living depend only on institutions

questions.explanation: Because **ideas and inventions flow more easily than institutions**, poor countries can import health and education gains quickly. Living standards (life expectancy, literacy) can rise even where real GDP per capita grows slowly.

questions.prompt: What does an increase in capital per hour worked, holding technology constant, do to real GDP per hour worked?

options.text: It shifts the whole production function upward
It moves the economy along the same production function, up and to the right, to a higher Y/L, but by progressively smaller amounts
It shifts the production function downward because of depreciation
It leaves Y/L unchanged because only technology matters

questions.explanation: More capital per hour worked is a **movement along** the unchanged per-worker production function. Because of diminishing returns to capital the curve gets flatter, so each additional unit of capital adds less to Y/L.

questions.prompt: What does an increase in technology, holding K/L constant, do to real GDP per hour worked?

options.text: It moves the economy along the same curve to the right
It shifts the production function downward
It shifts the production function upward, so Y/L is higher at every level of K/L
It makes the curve linear but does not change Y/L at the current K/L

questions.explanation: Technological change raises output for given inputs, so the **entire per-worker production function shifts up**: at the same K/L, workers produce more.

questions.prompt: What are the consequences for growth of diminishing returns to capital?

options.text: Output per hour worked falls whenever capital per hour worked rises
Growth rates must rise as capital accumulates
Diminishing returns affect labour but not capital
Increasing capital per hour worked alone yields smaller and smaller gains in output per hour, so growth driven only by capital accumulation slows down

questions.explanation: **Diminishing returns** means each extra unit of capital per hour adds less output than the last, so an economy growing only by accumulating capital sees its growth rate fall.

questions.prompt: How are some economies able to maintain high growth rates despite diminishing returns to capital?

options.text: Continuing technological change (and rising human capital) keeps shifting the production function upward, offsetting diminishing returns
By saving 100% of income so that capital stops depreciating
By moving along the production function faster
They cannot; no economy has ever maintained high growth

questions.explanation: Technological change shifts the per-worker production function up, so each new unit of capital is more productive and the economy **avoids running into diminishing returns**. That is why the model says long-run growth requires continuing technological progress.

questions.prompt: How does the new growth theory differ from the growth theory developed by Robert Solow?

options.text: New growth theory says capital accumulation alone can generate unlimited growth; Solow's says technology alone does

New growth theory explains technological change as the result of individuals' and firms' responses to economic incentives (R&D, learning by doing); Solow's model takes the growth of technology as given
New growth theory ignores technology and focuses on population; Solow's focuses on technology
They are the same model with different names

questions.explanation: In the Solow(–Swan) model **technology (A) is exogenous**: the model does not explain why it grows. The **new growth theory** treats technological change as an outcome of incentives, such as profit from R&D, knowledge capital and learning by doing, so policy can influence long-run growth.

questions.prompt: What is knowledge capital?

options.text: The total amount of money a country has saved
The skills workers acquire through on-the-job training only
The stock of ideas, discoveries and know-how (new products and ways of producing them) accumulated through research and development
The value of buildings and equipment used by universities

questions.explanation: **Knowledge capital** is the accumulated stock of inventions, research results and know-how. In new growth theory it is a central input to technological progress.

questions.prompt: Why are firms likely to underinvest in research and development?

options.text: R&D is unprofitable for every firm
Firms prefer to hold cash rather than invest
The government prohibits private research
Knowledge spills over to other firms that can copy it without paying, so the firm bears the full cost but captures only part of the benefits (a positive externality)

questions.explanation: R&D creates a **positive externality**: competitors imitate the new knowledge, so the social return exceeds the private return and firms invest less than is socially optimal.

questions.prompt: Which set contains three government policies that can increase the accumulation of knowledge capital?

options.text: Granting patents, giving tax incentives for private R&D, and subsidizing university and basic research
Price controls, higher tariffs and import quotas
Raising payroll taxes, shortening patent protection and cutting education funding
Printing money, taxing saving and restricting foreign investment

questions.explanation: Governments can raise knowledge capital by **protecting inventors (patents), lowering the cost of R&D (tax credits), and funding research** at universities and labs. The other sets would weaken innovation incentives or are unrelated.

questions.prompt: In 2023 the Economist said there are good reasons to be gloomy about Chinese workers' productivity and that many analysts cut their long-term forecasts for China's growth. Is there a connection?

options.text: No: productivity affects only unemployment, not growth
Yes: long-run growth in real GDP per capita depends on labour productivity growth, so weak productivity prospects lower long-run growth forecasts
Yes, but only because lower productivity raises population
No: growth forecasts depend only on the capital stock, not productivity

questions.explanation: In the growth model **growth in output per person comes from growth in labour productivity** (more K/L, better technology, more human capital). If productivity growth is expected to be low, long-run growth forecasts must be cut.

questions.prompt: Capital per hour worked increases from 200 yuan per hour worked to 250 yuan per hour worked.

options.text: An upward shift of the production function
A downward shift of the production function
A movement along the production function
A shift, but only if labour also increases

questions.explanation: A change in K/L, the variable on the horizontal axis, is a **movement along** the existing curve.

questions.prompt: The Chinese government doubles its spending on support for university research.

options.text: A movement along the production function
A downward shift of the production function
No effect on the production function
An upward shift of the production function, since more research raises technology

questions.explanation: Research spending raises knowledge capital and **technological progress**, which shifts the per-worker production function up (although the effect takes time).

questions.prompt: A reform of the Chinese school system results in more highly trained Chinese workers.

options.text: An upward shift of the production function, since human capital is higher
A movement along the production function
A downward shift of the production function
A change only in the capital stock

questions.explanation: Better-trained workers raise **human capital**, which increases Y/L at every level of K/L and shifts the production function up.

questions.prompt: Why did the investment decisions of salaried managers in the United States tend to be better for long-term growth than those of salaried bureaucrats in the Soviet Union?

options.text: US managers are simply more intelligent than Soviet bureaucrats

US managers answer to shareholders, capital markets and competitors, so poor investments are punished with losses and good ones rewarded with profits; Soviet bureaucrats faced no comparable market discipline
Soviet bureaucrats invested too little in physical capital
US managers can ignore shareholders because the money is not their own

questions.explanation: Even though managers spend others' money, in a market economy **profits and losses, competition and the threat of dismissal or takeover** discipline their choices. In the Soviet system, planners allocated resources by directive without market signals, so there was little incentive to adopt productive technologies.

questions.prompt: In 1961, why might a leading economist have expected the Soviet economy to eventually become larger than the US economy?

options.text: Soviet labour productivity already exceeded the US level
Soviet technology was far ahead of US technology
The Soviet Union was growing very rapidly by devoting huge resources to capital accumulation (very high investment rates) and shifting workers into industry
Soviet consumption per person was higher than in the United States

questions.explanation: Soviet growth in the 1950s was fast because of **extremely high rates of investment and rapid growth of labour and capital inputs**; extrapolating those growth rates made overtaking the United States seem plausible.

questions.prompt: Briefly explain why the Soviet economy failed to overtake the US economy.

options.text: Soviet saving rates were too low to accumulate capital
Soviet growth was faster than US growth in every year, but the Soviet starting point was too low
The Soviet Union grew too slowly in its first decade, and it never recovered
Growth based on capital accumulation alone ran into diminishing returns, and without market incentives there was little technological change to offset them

questions.explanation: Without technological change, **diminishing returns to capital** caused Soviet growth to slow. Central planning provided weak incentives for innovation and efficient investment, so rapid growth could not be sustained.

source.note: Graph read as having A, B, C at the same K/L on three successively higher curves.

questions.prompt: The movement from point A to point B shows the effects of technological change.
questions.explanation: A and B have the same K/L, but B lies on a higher production function, so Y/L rises with no change in capital. That is a **shift of the production function**: technological change (or higher human capital).

questions.prompt: The economy can move from point B to point C only if there are no diminishing returns to capital.
questions.explanation: B to C is another upward shift (technological change) at the same K/L. Diminishing returns concern movements *along* a curve, so they do not prevent a move from B to C.

source.note: Graph read as having A, B, C at the same K/L on three successively higher curves (see the scenario). If the textbook figure instead had A and C at different K/L, the answer to this part would change; check the figure.

questions.prompt: To move from point A to point C, the economy must increase the amount of capital per hour worked and experience technological change.
questions.explanation: A and C have the same K/L, so no change in capital per hour is needed. The move is entirely a **shift up** due to technological change.

source.note: The textbook figure is described only as a curve rising steeply from the origin. The stem here states explicitly that the curve does not flatten (no diminishing returns), which is the point of the problem, so the reading does not depend on the word 'steep'.

questions.prompt: Suppose the per-worker production function were an upward-sloping curve that does not flatten as capital per hour worked rises (it rises steeply from the origin, with no diminishing returns). What would this imply for a country accumulating increasing quantities of capital per hour worked?

options.text: Capital accumulation alone could keep raising output per hour worked at a steady (or accelerating) pace, so growth could be sustained without technological change
Growth would still have to stop eventually, because diminishing returns always set in
Output per hour worked would fall as K/L rises
Growth would require the population to fall

questions.explanation: In the standard model, growth driven by capital alone must slow because of **diminishing returns**. If the curve does not flatten, each additional unit of capital keeps adding as much (or more) output, so growth from capital accumulation could be sustained. Real economies do not look like this, which is why technological change matters.

questions.prompt: Soviet growth strategy relied on very high rates of investment, causing rapid growth of the capital stock. Why was this a poor way to sustain growth in the long run?

options.text: High investment always lowers output
Without technological change, diminishing returns to capital meant each additional unit of capital added less output, so growth slowed
Capital accumulation makes technology disappear
Soviet investment was too low to matter

questions.explanation: Rapid capital accumulation moves the economy along its per-worker production function, where **diminishing returns** make each new unit of capital less productive. Sustained growth requires technological progress, which the Soviet system did not generate.

questions.prompt: What success are the authors referring to, and why might creative destruction be the key to it?

options.text: America's low unemployment; creative destruction prevents firms from failing
America's trade surplus; creative destruction reduces imports
America's high long-run growth and living standards; creative destruction brings continual innovation, replacing old products and firms with more productive ones
America's equal income distribution; creative destruction removes high earners

questions.explanation: The success is **sustained economic growth and high living standards**. Creative destruction is how new technologies and products replace old ones, continually raising productivity.

questions.prompt: Why does creative destruction need to be “tolerated”? If it leads to a country's success, shouldn't everyone support it?

options.text: Because it reduces total output in the long run
Because it makes everyone worse off
Because it has no winners
Because it also destroys existing firms and jobs, creating concentrated losers who may resist it even though society as a whole gains

questions.explanation: The gains are spread across the economy while the losses (closed firms, displaced workers) are concentrated, so losers have strong incentives to resist. Societies must **tolerate the losses** to get the long-run gains.

questions.prompt: Briefly explain Romer's reasoning.

options.text: Ideas can be used by everyone at no additional cost, so more people means more potential discoveries that benefit all, beyond the gains from comparative advantage
Trade is beneficial only if the other country has a comparative advantage in every good
Population growth always reduces per capita incomes
Other countries' discoveries cannot be copied

questions.explanation: Under the standard argument, Portugal matters because of comparative advantage. In new growth theory, **ideas are non-rival**: a discovery by anyone raises productivity everywhere, so more people means more ideas for all.

questions.prompt: Is the existence of the Portuguese more important in the new growth theory or in Solow's original model?

options.text: In Solow's model, because population drives technology
In the new growth theory, because technological change comes from people responding to incentives; in Solow's model technology is given
Equally important in both
Neither, because both ignore population

questions.explanation: In Solow's model technological progress is **exogenous**, so more people do not add to it. In the new growth theory, more people mean more researchers and more ideas, so population matters more.

questions.prompt: Which description best captures the record of productivity growth in Canada from 1870 to the present?

options.text: Steady growth at the same rate in every period since 1870
Productivity fell continuously from 1870 to 1973 and has risen since
Rapid growth from after World War II to the mid-1970s, a slowdown of about 20 years, a pick-up from the mid-1990s for about a decade, and slower growth again recently
Growth was fastest between 2006 and 2020

questions.explanation: Canadian growth followed several phases: strong postwar growth, **a long slowdown (mid-1970s to mid-1990s)**, an IT-driven rebound (mid-1990s–2005), and historically weak growth since 2006.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the debate among economists over future Canadian productivity growth?

options.text: Optimists think productivity will fall; pessimists think it will rise
Economists agree growth will return to postwar levels
The debate is only about the size of the labour force
Optimists think measurement problems hide real gains, or that new technologies like AI will boost productivity; pessimists think the big gains from the IT revolution are over and growth will stay low

questions.explanation: **Optimists**: productivity is mismeasured and new technologies will help. **Pessimists**: the easy IT gains are exhausted and factors like aging and regulation hold growth down.

questions.prompt: Figure 7.5 shows growth in real GDP per person in Canada since 1870. How might the growth rates differ if calculated for real GDP per hour worked instead?

options.text: They would generally be higher, because hours worked per person have fallen since 1870 (shorter work weeks, more years in school and retirement)
They would be lower, because hours worked per person have risen since 1870
They would be identical
They would be negative

questions.explanation: Y/population = (Y/hours) × (hours/population). If **hours per person have fallen**, output per hour has grown faster than output per person.

questions.prompt: A columnist notes that many economists expect GDP growth to stay around 2% and that productivity growth has slowed markedly with no sign of a sudden upturn. Is there a connection?

options.text: No: GDP growth does not depend on productivity
Yes: long-run GDP growth depends on growth in labour and in labour productivity, so if productivity growth stays low, GDP growth stays low
Yes: low productivity growth raises GDP growth
No: productivity affects only inflation

questions.explanation: Growth in real GDP comes from more labour and **more output per worker**. If productivity growth is weak and no new surge is expected, GDP growth stays low.

questions.prompt: Robert Gordon argues that most of the economy has already benefited from the internet and that many jobs are outside the capabilities of AI and robots. If he is correct, what does this imply for future Canadian labour productivity growth?

options.text: It will be very high, because AI will transform all jobs
It will fall to zero because of depreciation
Productivity growth is likely to remain low, since the large IT gains are exhausted and AI will affect only part of the economy
It will be unaffected by technology

questions.explanation: Gordon is a **pessimist**: the main gains from the IT revolution are behind us and much of the economy (services done by hand) has little scope for technological change, so productivity growth is likely to stay low.

questions.prompt: Are the benefits to you of being able to do a Google search included in GDP?

options.text: Yes, the full value of the benefit is counted
Yes, because Google's profits include the entire value to users
No, because GDP includes only goods, not services
Largely not: the search is free, so its value to users is not captured by market prices and is not counted in GDP

questions.explanation: GDP counts the **market value of final goods and services**. A free service generates no price × quantity for users, so most of the benefit is not measured.

questions.prompt: Does this show that the slowdown in Canadian productivity growth is just a measurement problem? What information would be needed to decide?

options.text: Not necessarily: we would need to know whether unmeasured benefits have grown enough, relative to earlier periods, to explain the size of the measured slowdown
Yes, it proves productivity growth has not slowed
No, because mismeasurement never happens
Yes, because services cannot be measured at all

questions.explanation: Unmeasured benefits existed in earlier eras too (e.g., earlier technologies), so the issue is whether **unmeasured benefits have grown enough** to account for the measured slowdown. That requires data on the value of unmeasured improvements over time.

questions.prompt: Briefly, what is secular stagnation?

options.text: A temporary recession lasting less than a year
A prolonged period of weak economic growth and weak private demand, with persistently low interest rates
A period of high inflation and fast growth
The permanent disappearance of unemployment

questions.explanation: Alvin Hansen (1938) used the term for chronic, **structurally weak private demand** that leaves growth low for long periods.

questions.prompt: In the market for loanable funds, how does secular stagnation shift the demand for and supply of loanable funds?

options.text: Demand shifts right and supply shifts left
Both shift right
Demand shifts left (fewer profitable investment opportunities) and supply shifts right (higher desired saving)
Both shift left

questions.explanation: Stagnation means **less desire to invest** (demand for funds falls) and often **more desire to save**, e.g., with aging populations (supply of funds rises).

questions.prompt: What happens to the equilibrium interest rate and quantity of loanable funds?

options.text: Both the interest rate and quantity rise
The interest rate rises and the quantity falls
The interest rate is unchanged and the quantity rises
The interest rate falls; the equilibrium quantity could rise or fall depending on the sizes of the shifts

questions.explanation: Leftward demand and rightward supply both lower the equilibrium interest rate, but they push the quantity in opposite directions, so the **quantity change is ambiguous**.

questions.prompt: What does Blanchard mean by “structurally low private demand,” and why might it be structural?

options.text: Persistently weak consumption and investment spending by the private sector that does not go away with the business cycle, caused by long-lasting forces such as aging and weak investment opportunities
Private demand that falls temporarily during a recession
Private demand that exceeds government demand
Demand for structures such as buildings

questions.explanation: ‘Structural’ means **long-lasting rather than cyclical**: demographic and technological forces keep private spending low.

questions.prompt: Why might structurally low private demand result in secular stagnation?

options.text: Low demand raises interest rates and encourages investment
Low spending depresses investment and output, and interest rates fall toward zero, leaving central banks little room to stimulate demand, so weak growth persists
Low demand increases the supply of goods and so raises output
It cannot; low demand has no lasting effect

questions.explanation: Weak demand reduces output and investment, while interest rates near their lower bound limit **monetary policy's ability to restore demand**.

questions.prompt: Which are examples of deep structural factors that might lead to secular stagnation in Canada?

options.text: A young, fast-growing population and rapid productivity growth
Persistent high inflation
An aging population, slow productivity growth and weak investment opportunities, and rising inequality that raises saving
A sudden fall in oil prices

questions.explanation: Aging societies save more and invest less, slow technological progress reduces the return to investment, and inequality shifts income to high savers. **All lower demand structurally.**

questions.prompt: Why does the economic growth model predict that poor countries should catch up to rich countries in real GDP per capita?

options.text: Poor countries have more capital per worker
Poor countries have higher levels of technology
Rich countries' growth rates always rise over time
Poor countries have less capital per hour worked, so extra capital yields larger output gains (diminishing returns), and they can adopt existing technology from richer countries

questions.explanation: The model predicts **catch-up (convergence)**: poor countries start lower on the production function, where diminishing returns mean capital is more productive, and they can copy existing technology, so they grow faster. This prediction holds for countries with similar institutions and conditions for growth; where those differ (rule of law, stability, education), catch-up need not happen.

questions.prompt: Why have some poor countries not been able to catch up?

options.text: Wars and revolutions, poor education and health, weak rule of law, and low saving and investment
Excessive foreign investment
Too much globalization
Too much capital per worker

questions.explanation: The four obstacles are **wars/instability, poor education and health, lack of rule of law, and low saving/investment**.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between foreign direct investment and foreign portfolio investment?

options.text: FDI is buying stocks and bonds; foreign portfolio investment is building a factory
FDI is a firm building or buying a facility in another country; foreign portfolio investment is an individual or firm buying stocks or bonds issued in another country
They are the same thing
FDI is government aid; foreign portfolio investment is private lending

questions.explanation: **FDI = a physical presence** (factory, store, purchase of a business). **Foreign portfolio investment = financial securities** (shares, bonds).

questions.prompt: How might a poor country benefit from them?

options.text: They reduce the capital stock
They benefit only rich countries
Both bring in funds for investment, raising capital per worker; FDI also brings in technology and management know-how
They bring only debt and no benefits

questions.explanation: Foreign funds raise **domestic investment** beyond what low domestic saving would permit, and FDI also transfers technology.

questions.prompt: What does globalization mean?

options.text: Countries closing their borders to protect industries
The adoption of a single world currency
Governments setting world prices
The process of countries becoming more open to foreign trade and investment, and more interconnected economically

questions.explanation: **Globalization** is increased openness to trade, investment, technology and ideas across borders.

questions.prompt: How have developing countries benefited from globalization?

options.text: Access to foreign capital, technology and larger markets has helped them grow faster (e.g., countries that opened up since the 1980s)
Higher tariffs protected their industries and always raised growth
Countries that closed their economies grew fastest
They gained nothing

questions.explanation: Countries that **opened to trade and foreign investment** gained technology and capital; those that restricted trade (1940s–1970s) grew slowly.

source.note: Table values from the textbook. Figure-based Problem 4.5 is not included (scatterplot not reproducible).

questions.prompt: The table shows 1960 real GDP per capita and 1960–2019 growth for: Botswana ($519, 6.10%), Uganda ($940, 1.31%), Madagascar ($1,657, −0.17%), Ireland ($7,065, 4.64%) and the United States ($19,365, 2.01%). Are these statistics consistent with the growth model's prediction of catch-up?

options.text: Fully consistent: the poorer the country, the faster it grew
Partly: Botswana and Ireland started below the US and grew faster, but Uganda and Madagascar, also poor, grew slowly, so catch-up is not automatic
Completely inconsistent: no poor country grew faster than the United States
Consistent, because the richest country grew fastest

questions.explanation: The model predicts that poorer countries tend to grow faster. Botswana (poorest, fastest) and Ireland fit, but **Uganda and Madagascar did not catch up**, showing that catch-up depends on institutions, education, stability and investment.

source.note: Graphs 1 and 3 are close; matching based on the pattern of Figures 7.7–7.9.

questions.prompt: Which graph best depicts all countries for which statistics are available, 1960–2019?

options.text: Graph 1 (flat)
Graph 2 (downward-sloping)
Graph 3 (slightly upward-sloping)
None of the graphs

questions.explanation: Across all countries there is **no catch-up**: many poor countries did not grow faster, and the average relationship is flat to slightly upward (Figure 7.8).

source.note: Graphs 1 and 3 are close; matching based on the pattern of Figures 7.8-7.9 (no catch-up since 1990 means growth unrelated to initial income).

questions.prompt: Which graph best depicts the United States, Western Europe, Canada and Japan, 1990–2019?

options.text: Graph 2 (downward-sloping)
Graph 3 (slightly upward-sloping)
None of the graphs
Graph 1 (flat)

questions.explanation: Since 1990 these high-income countries **stopped catching up**: growth was unrelated to initial income (Figure 7.9).

questions.prompt: Which graph best depicts current high-income countries, 1960–2019?

options.text: Graph 2 (downward-sloping)
Graph 1 (flat)
Graph 3 (slightly upward-sloping)
None of the graphs

questions.explanation: Among today's high-income countries, those poorer in 1960 (South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong) grew fastest: **clear catch-up** (Figure 7.7).

questions.prompt: What does McCloskey mean by “thoroughgoing innovation” and by getting “within hailing distance of the West”?

options.text: Banning foreign ideas; becoming richer than the West
Widely adopting new technologies, ideas and ways of organizing production; and reaching a standard of living close to (not necessarily equal to) that of high-income countries
Borrowing money from the West; having an identical income
Reducing population; matching military power

questions.explanation: ‘Thoroughgoing innovation’ is broad, sustained adoption of new technologies and institutions; ‘hailing distance’ means **being close to rich-country living standards**.

questions.prompt: What would Haiti's real GDP per capita be in 2071 (2010 US dollars)?
Would Haiti end up with the real GDP per capita that Italy enjoyed in 2021?

options.text: Yes, it would more than double Italy's level
Yes, exactly
No, but it would be close: about $29,900 against $31,506
No, it would be less than half

questions.explanation: $29,902 is **about 95% of Italy's 2021 level**: ‘within hailing distance’ but not equal (it would need about 6.6% a year to match).

questions.prompt: McCloskey also notes that this “does not mean that catch-up is inevitable.” Why isn't catch-up inevitable?

options.text: Technology cannot be copied
Rich countries refuse to trade
Catch-up requires lower saving
Poor countries may lack the rule of law, stability, education and health, and investment needed to adopt and benefit from technology

questions.explanation: Catch-up depends on the **conditions for growth** (property rights, stability, human capital, investment). Many poor countries lack them.

questions.prompt: Is the forecast likely for growth in nominal GDP or real GDP?

options.text: Real GDP: growth forecasts refer to real output, and 2.3% would be a very low forecast for nominal GDP when inflation is high
Nominal GDP, since it includes inflation
Neither; it is a forecast of population
Nominal GDP, because it is easier to forecast

questions.explanation: Real GDP growth measures changes in output, which is what matters for living standards, and central bank growth forecasts are normally **in real terms**.

questions.prompt: Given your answer, is per capita GDP likely to expand more quickly or more slowly than 2.3%?

options.text: More quickly, because dividing by population always raises growth
More slowly, if the population is growing (per capita growth ≈ GDP growth − population growth)
The same, always
More quickly, because the population is shrinking

questions.explanation: Real GDP per capita growth ≈ **real GDP growth − population growth**. With positive population growth, per capita growth is smaller than 2.3%.

questions.prompt: Assuming the forecast is accurate, did living standards in Mexico likely rise or fall in 2023?

options.text: Fell, because forecasts are always too high
Rose, and no additional information is needed
Likely rose, since 2.3% real GDP growth probably exceeds population growth; to be more confident we would need Mexico's population growth rate (and how the gains were distributed)
Fell, because growth was below 2.5%

questions.explanation: 2.3% growth in real GDP probably exceeds population growth, so real GDP per capita likely rose. We need the **population growth rate** (and information on distribution) to be sure.

source.note: Textbook data on Mexico's growth since 1980 are summarized qualitatively here.

questions.prompt: How does a 4% growth rate compare with the growth rate Mexico has experienced since 1980?

options.text: It is about the same as Mexico's experience
It is well below what Mexico has experienced
Mexico has not grown at all since 1980
It is well above what Mexico has experienced; Mexico's growth since 1980 has been much slower

questions.explanation: Mexico's growth since 1980 has been **modest, well below 4%**, and well below the growth of fast-growing Asian economies such as China, so 4% would be a large improvement.

questions.prompt: What are business-friendly policies and infrastructure, and why would Levy expect them to have such a large effect on growth?

options.text: Business-friendly policies cut regulation and uncertainty so firms invest; infrastructure is roads, ports and power. Both raise the productivity of private capital and labour and attract investment
Policies that tax business; infrastructure means housing; they would reduce growth
Policies that ban imports; infrastructure means machinery; they would raise prices
They are identical terms with no growth effects

questions.explanation: **Infrastructure** (roads, ports, electricity, telecom) raises productivity, and **business-friendly policies** raise the return to investment; both increase K/L and A.

source.note: Judgment question; most defensible reading chosen.

questions.prompt: Is foreign investment important to increasing Mexico's growth, and is it as important to Canadian economic growth?

options.text: Unimportant for both
It is important to Mexico because of low domestic saving; it matters less for Canada, which has higher saving and well-developed capital markets
More important for Canada than for Mexico
Equally and entirely important to both

questions.explanation: Foreign investment gives countries with **low domestic saving** access to capital and technology. Canada has more domestic saving and deep financial markets, though it still benefits.

questions.prompt: Why would countries that isolate themselves rather than participate fully in the global economy hurt their own people?

options.text: Isolation raises productivity by protecting domestic firms
Isolation eliminates diminishing returns
They lose access to foreign markets, capital, technology and cheaper goods, which reduces growth and living standards
Isolation increases foreign investment

questions.explanation: Open economies gain **larger markets, foreign capital and technology and specialization**; closed economies (1940s–1970s) grew slowly.

questions.prompt: Is there an argument that globalization hurts rather than helps some economies?

options.text: No: globalization makes everyone better off
Yes: globalization reduces total output for every country
No: globalization only affects financial markets
Yes: workers and firms in industries facing import competition can lose jobs and income, and some countries may struggle to compete, even though the gains are larger overall

questions.explanation: Globalization creates **winners and losers**: import-competing industries and their workers lose, though the gains to consumers and exporters are typically larger.

questions.prompt: Which people and industries around the world were likely hurt the most by this reduction in trade?

options.text: Exporting industries and their workers, and consumers and firms that depend on imports; especially developing countries relying on export markets
Domestic firms protected from import competition
Governments that collect tariffs
No one, since trade has no effect on incomes

questions.explanation: Lower trade reduces demand for exports and raises the cost of imported goods, hurting **exporters, their workers, and consumers**, especially in export-dependent developing economies.

questions.prompt: Are there people and industries that benefit when world trade declines?

options.text: No: everyone loses from reduced trade
Yes: domestic firms and workers in import-competing industries, who face less foreign competition
Yes: all exporting firms
Yes: all consumers

questions.explanation: Less trade reduces competition for **import-competing industries**, protecting their sales and jobs, although consumers and exporters lose.

source.note: The textbook says there are no definite answers; the most defensible reading based on the chapter's model is chosen.

questions.prompt: The Roman Empire built impressive monuments and aqueducts but did not experience sustained economic growth. Which explanation is most consistent with the growth model and new growth theory?

options.text: Rome lacked any physical capital
Rome had too much technological progress
Roman institutions provided weak incentives for continuing innovation and investment (little institutionalized technological change), so growth spurts did not last
Rome grew too fast and ran out of labour

questions.explanation: Sustained growth needs **continuing technological change**, which depends on incentives and institutions (property rights, markets for ideas, R&D). Without those, periods of growth were short-lived.

questions.prompt: Which set contains three government policies that can increase economic growth?

options.text: Price controls, tariffs and import quotas
Raising payroll taxes, shortening patents and cutting schooling budgets
Printing more money, restricting trade and limiting foreign investment
Enforcing property rights and the rule of law, improving health and education, and providing incentives for saving and investment (or subsidizing R&D)

questions.explanation: Growth-promoting policies: **property rights/rule of law, health and education, technology/R&D support, and saving/investment incentives**.

questions.prompt: Has economic analysis determined that economic growth will always improve economic well-being?

options.text: No: whether continued growth is desirable is a normative question that economic analysis cannot settle
Yes, growth always raises well-being for everyone
Yes, because GDP measures well-being perfectly
No, because growth never raises incomes

questions.explanation: Economics can say how to raise growth (a positive question), but whether more growth is desirable involves **value judgments (normative)**, including environmental costs and distribution.

questions.prompt: Why might replacing legal restrictions on firing workers with unemployment insurance increase economic growth?

options.text: Firms would hire fewer workers
Firms would be more willing to hire and to reallocate workers to more productive uses, while workers remain protected by insurance
It would keep workers in low-productivity jobs
It would reduce competition

questions.explanation: Firing restrictions make firms reluctant to hire and trap workers in low-productivity firms. **Unemployment insurance protects workers without blocking the reallocation** of labour to more productive uses.

questions.prompt: What are possible negative effects of taxing business payrolls rather than taxing incomes?

options.text: They raise employment
They have no effect on hiring
Payroll taxes raise the cost of hiring, discouraging employment (especially formal jobs) and lowering output
They reduce the cost of labour

questions.explanation: A tax on payrolls raises the effective cost of labour, **reducing hiring** and encouraging informal employment.

questions.prompt: What is a “tax perk,” and why might perks for small firms slow growth?

options.text: A tax increase on large firms; it helps small firms become more productive
A subsidy for imports; it helps large firms
A tax refund for consumers; it has no effect on firms
A special tax break; perks for small firms encourage firms to stay small rather than grow, even though larger firms are typically more productive

questions.explanation: Tax perks that disappear as firms grow create an incentive to **stay small**. Levy assumes larger firms are more productive, so keeping firms small lowers productivity and growth.

questions.prompt: What does Levy mean by “contract enforcement,” and why might better enforcement increase growth?

options.text: Courts and government ensuring that agreements are honoured; it gives firms the confidence to invest, trade and lend
Forcing people to sign contracts; it reduces trade
Banning contracts between firms; it increases competition
Setting prices by contract; it reduces uncertainty

questions.explanation: Part of the **rule of law**: if contracts are enforced, entrepreneurs and lenders can rely on agreements, boosting investment and trade.

questions.prompt: How might spending on building residential property increase economic growth in the short run?

options.text: It permanently raises technology
Construction spending adds to demand and output and creates jobs now
It reduces investment
It lowers output in the short run

questions.explanation: Residential construction raises **current output and employment**, so measured growth rises in the short run.

questions.prompt: Why might investment in residential property not lead to long-term growth?

options.text: Housing raises K/L in production so it always raises productivity
Housing is a form of technology
Housing does not raise the productivity of workers in producing goods and services the way productive capital, technology or human capital does
Housing is not counted in GDP

questions.explanation: Long-term growth requires **higher labour productivity** (more productive capital per worker, technology, human capital). Apartments provide housing services but do not raise output per hour in other sectors.

questions.prompt: What does the author mean by “rule of law”?

options.text: Rule by decree
A system with no laws
The fact that laws exist on paper
The ability of the government to enforce the laws, especially protecting property rights and enforcing contracts, with the government itself bound by the law

questions.explanation: The **rule of law** means laws are enforced impartially, protecting property rights and contracts.

questions.prompt: Why do economists believe a government must follow the rule of law for a country to achieve sustained growth?

options.text: Secure property rights and contract enforcement give entrepreneurs the confidence to invest and innovate, because they expect to keep the gains
Rule of law reduces investment
It increases corruption
It has no effect on growth

questions.explanation: Without it, entrepreneurs fear **seizure of gains** and unenforced contracts, discouraging investment and innovation.

source.note: The author of the article claims China lacks the rule of law; the question asks you to reason from that premise.

questions.prompt: If China doesn't follow the rule of law, what explains its high growth?

options.text: China has diminishing returns that don't apply to it

Both grew rapidly from a low base by mobilizing huge amounts of capital and labour. The Soviet Union relied on capital accumulation with little technological change, so growth ran into diminishing returns; China also opened to markets, foreign investment and foreign technology (catch-up). Growth without the rule of law may not be sustainable
China's high growth proves that rule of law is irrelevant
China grew by lowering investment

questions.explanation: Neither case shows that the rule of law is unnecessary for *sustained* growth. The USSR grew rapidly by mobilizing capital and labour under central planning, with little technological change, so diminishing returns eventually slowed it. China's growth also relied on very high investment, but it added market reforms, foreign investment and adoption of existing foreign technology, which let it catch up from a low base. Catch-up growth from a low base can be fast without the rule of law, but sustaining it for a long period is doubtful.

questions.prompt: The government passes an investment tax credit, which reduces a firm's taxes if it installs new machinery, equipment or software.

options.text: Likely to reduce growth
No effect on growth
Likely to increase growth: it encourages investment, raising capital per hour worked (and embodying new technology)
Likely to reduce investment

questions.explanation: Lower after-tax cost of capital → **more investment in new machinery and software**, raising K/L and embodied technology.

questions.prompt: The government shortens the period of patent protection for new inventions.

options.text: Likely to increase growth by increasing R&D
Likely to increase growth by lowering prices forever
No effect on innovation
Not likely to increase growth: it reduces the reward to innovators and so reduces incentives for R&D

questions.explanation: Patents protect the profit from inventions; **shorter patent protection lowers the incentive** to do R&D, so growth would, if anything, fall.

questions.prompt: The government provides more funds for low-interest loans to college students.

options.text: Likely to increase growth: it raises human capital by increasing the number of educated workers
Likely to reduce growth
No effect on productivity
Likely to reduce human capital

questions.explanation: More education raises **human capital** and therefore productivity.

questions.prompt: Why would a free press be vital for enhancing property rights and the rule of law?

options.text: It allows the government to control information
It exposes government and court abuses, such as property seizures, so officials are held accountable
It reduces the number of laws
It prevents trade

questions.explanation: A free press **monitors the government** and publicizes violations of property rights.

questions.prompt: How could a free press help reduce corruption?

options.text: By paying officials
By hiding information
By investigating and publicizing corrupt behaviour, raising the risk and cost of corruption
By banning investigations

questions.explanation: Publicity raises the **probability of being caught**, discouraging corruption.

questions.prompt: What type of aid was Adesina most likely referring to?

options.text: Foreign direct investment by firms
Domestic saving
International trade
Foreign aid: transfers of funds or goods from rich-country governments and organizations to poor-country governments or people

questions.explanation: **Aid** means transfers (grants, assistance) from governments and international organizations.

questions.prompt: What type of investment was he referring to, and why might he believe it matters more than aid?

options.text: Foreign direct investment and portfolio investment: they add productive capital and technology and create jobs, whereas aid can be wasted or lost to corruption and doesn't create productive capacity
Investment in housing only; aid creates capital
Domestic government spending; aid is more productive
Investment in stocks by Africans only; aid has no effect

questions.explanation: Private investment raises **K/L and brings technology**, and it responds to returns rather than politics; aid often fails to raise productivity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most likely true of the effects of the tariffs?

options.text: All US firms gained
US firms competing with Chinese imports (and their workers) likely gained, while US firms that use imported inputs and US consumers likely lost
All US consumers gained from lower prices
US firms that import inputs gained the most

questions.explanation: Tariffs **raise the price of imports**, benefiting import-competing producers and workers but hurting consumers and firms that use imported inputs.

questions.prompt: If the tariffs remained in place for years, would they affect the long-run growth rate of the US economy?

options.text: Raise it by increasing investment
No effect
Probably lower it: tariffs raise the cost of imported capital goods and technology, reduce competition and discourage investment
Raise it because prices rise

questions.explanation: Anti-globalization policies **limit access to foreign capital and technology and increase uncertainty**, hurting investment and growth.
